extracted.intended_audience: analysts in U.S. Federal regulatory agencies preparing regulatory analyses / RIAs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analyses (benefit-cost and cost-effectiveness analyses) to support major and other rulemakings by U.S. federal agencies, including required documentation, accounting statements, and specialized statutory analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis is a tool regulatory agencies use to anticipate and evaluate the likely consequences of rules; it organizes evidence on the key effects—good and bad—of alternatives to learn if benefits justify costs and to discover the most cost-effective alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good regulatory analysis is designed to inform the public and other parts of Government and should sometimes show a proposed action is misguided or that well-conceived actions are reasonable and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three key elements of a regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the basic elements that any regulatory analysis should contain; evaluations should cover both proposed action and the main alternatives identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain causal linkage from actions to benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the actions required by the rule are linked to the expected benefits (for example, indicate how additional safety equipment will reduce safety risks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform a similar causal analysis for each alternative considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a clear baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits and costs are defined in comparison with a clearly stated alternative, normally a 'no action' baseline: what the world will be like if the proposed rule is not adopted. Comparisons to a 'next best' alternative are also useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the baseline explicitly so readers understand the incremental impacts being measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify side-effects and ancillary benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify expected undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits of the proposed regulatory action and the alternatives; these should be added to direct benefits and costs as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both direct and ancillary effects in estimates where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify monetized, quantified-but-not-monetized, and qualitative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Report benefit and cost estimates in three mutually exclusive categories: monetized/quantified, quantified but not monetized, and qualitative (not quantified or monetized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a summary of estimates for each alternative including qualitative and non-monetized factors so readers can evaluate them; avoid double-counting across categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of non-quantified benefits and costs (threshold/break-even analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: When important benefits/costs cannot be expressed in monetary units, use professional judgment to assess their importance and carry out a 'threshold' or 'break-even' analysis to evaluate their significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threshold analysis answers how small the non-quantified benefits could be (or how large costs would need to be) before net benefits equal zero; indicate which non-quantified effects are most important and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek out opinions of those who will be affected by the regulation and those with special knowledge or insight; consultation should occur early and not be limited to the final stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early consultation helps ensure relevant issues and pertinent data are addressed and available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use competent professional judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Conducting high-quality analysis requires competent professional judgment; different regulations may call for different emphases depending on nature, complexity, and sensitivity to assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts cannot follow a strict formula for every case; tailor methods and emphasis to the context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of assumptions and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis is transparent: state assumptions used (time horizon, discount rates, etc.), provide sensitivity analysis, and make it possible for a qualified third party to see how estimates and conclusions were derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific references to all data sources, appendices documenting models, and results of formal sensitivity and uncertainty analyses; include an executive summary and a standardized accounting statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate necessity for federal regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, agencies must demonstrate the proposed action is necessary; if action results from statutory or judicial directive, describe specific authority, extent of discretion, and regulatory instruments available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether action addresses a significant market failure or other compelling public need, and assess the significance qualitatively and where feasible quantitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and document market failures or other social purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: If regulation is designed to correct a market failure, describe the failure (externality, market power, inadequate/asymmetric information) qualitatively and quantitatively where feasible; other justifications include improving government functioning, redistribution, anti-discrimination, privacy, or promoting personal freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that government intervention is likely to do more good than harm; for information-processing mistakes or asymmetric information, document carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider non-regulatory and lower-level alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Before choosing Federal regulation, consider alternatives such as antitrust enforcement, consumer litigation, administrative compensation systems, State or local regulation, or other less intrusive interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether State/local action or nonregulatory measures would be more appropriate given the nature and geographic scope of the problem; consider harmonization and international trade effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against certain types of economic regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A particularly demanding burden of proof is required to justify: price controls in competitive markets; production or sales quotas in competitive markets; mandatory uniform quality standards where voluntary standards or disclosure suffice; controls on entry into employment/production except where indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid regulations that increase market power for selected entities unless clearly warranted; recognize limited circumstances for validating a monopoly (natural monopoly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematically evaluate a range of alternative regulatory approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore modifications of attributes/provisions and consider a manageable number of alternatives for detailed analysis; the number is a matter of judgment balancing thoroughness and practical limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives to consider include different statutory choices, different compliance dates, different enforcement methods, different degrees of stringency, different requirements for firm sizes, different geographic requirements, performance vs design standards, market-oriented approaches, and informational measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different compliance dates as an alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternative compliance dates because timing can significantly affect net benefits (e.g., allowing lead time can reduce overall costs while delayed implementation may lose future benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how the schedule affects benefits and costs for regulated industries and the environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different enforcement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternative enforcement frameworks (on-site inspections, periodic reporting, penalties, random or parametric monitoring) and identify the most appropriate enforcement mix based on benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different monitoring/reporting methods may vary in cost and effectiveness; choose proportionate methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze different degrees of stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Study alternative levels of regulatory stringency to understand relationships between stringency and the size and distribution of benefits and costs among groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marginal costs generally increase with stringency, while marginal benefits may decrease; analyze incremental changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider differential requirements for firm size
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider setting different requirements for large and small firms, based on estimated differences in compliance costs or benefits, and account for Regulatory Flexibility Act requirements when impacts on many small entities are significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing heavier burdens on one segment solely because it can better afford higher costs; consult SBA Chief Counsel and agency RFA guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider regional differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where benefits and costs vary significantly by region, consider setting different requirements for different geographic areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh gains from diversity and local experimentation against costs of fragmented regulation (e.g., higher compliance costs for firms operating in multiple jurisdictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer performance standards to design standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance standards (requirements expressed in terms of outcomes) are generally superior because they give regulated parties flexibility to achieve objectives cost-effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for both cost savings from flexibility and potential monitoring/compliance assurance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider market-oriented approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore market-oriented instruments—fees, penalties, subsidies, marketable permits/offsets, changing liability or property rights, bonds/insurance/warranties—as alternatives to direct controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether mechanisms like averaging, banking, and trading (ABT) can reduce costs while avoiding unacceptable localized adverse outcomes (hot spots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider informational measures for information failures
rubrics_metrics.description: When market failures stem from inadequate or asymmetric information, prefer informational remedies (standardized testing/rating, disclosure requirements, government provision of information) when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the benefits and costs of informational measures, including displaced information, misinterpretation, compliance costs of gathering and communicating data, and incentives created by mandatory disclosure; consider least intrusive sufficient alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA) and Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use BCA and CEA as systematic frameworks; prepare CEA for major health/safety rulemakings where a valid effectiveness measure exists, and BCA for major rulemakings; when primary benefits cannot be monetized, do both when feasible; otherwise present qualitative discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of analytical consistency across regulations and agencies subject to statutory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for Benefit-Cost Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: BCA expresses benefits and costs in monetary units to evaluate options using a common measure; measure incremental benefits and costs of successively more stringent alternatives to identify the alternative that maximizes net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on benefit-cost ratios as indicators of net benefits; use net benefits (benefits minus costs) as the decision metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: CEA compares regulatory actions with the same primary outcome (or integrated outcomes) to identify the most effective use of resources without monetizing all benefits; prefer incremental CEA over average ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct cost and effectiveness measures carefully, include all relevant societal costs (public and private), avoid double-counting, and present incremental comparisons against the baseline and successive options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and justify effectiveness metrics for health and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Select one or more measures (lives saved, life-years saved, 'equivalent lives', QALYs) and explain their use; integrated measures capture morbidity and mortality impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use integrated measures when a rule affects both mortality and morbidity significantly; be aware of restrictive assumptions (e.g., QALY assumptions) and consider reporting multiple measures for perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and subgroup treatment in effectiveness measures
rubrics_metrics.description: When numeric adjustments are made for life expectancy or quality of life, prefer population averages rather than subgroup measures dominated by a demographic or income group; ensure fair treatment of all segments (e.g., disabled populations) in CEA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not diminish life-years saved for disabled populations simply because of higher disability prevalence; base life expectancy on average cohorts where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present multiple measures and explain selection
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB encourages agencies to report results with multiple measures of effectiveness that offer different insights and to explain which measures were selected and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing multiple measures increases transparency and understanding of tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of benefits and costs over time (discounting and reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of estimates for each year of the analytic horizon and present annualized benefits and costs using real discount rates of 3% and 7%; report all monetized effects in 2001 dollars using the GDP deflator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streams should begin in the year the final rule will begin to have effects; report undiscounted yearly streams and annualized figures for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of risk and uncertainty and sensitivity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates and distributions where possible; supply upper and lower bounds (preferably 95% and 5% confidence bounds) and conduct sensitivity analysis to reveal how results depend on assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensitivity to find 'switch points' and vary one or combinations of variables; where uncertainty is critical, describe benefits and costs under plausible alternative assumptions and include footnotes/warnings in tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal probabilistic analysis for complex or very large rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply formal probabilistic analysis (simulation models, expert elicitation, Monte Carlo) for complex rules with large uncertainties or for rules exceeding the $1 billion annual threshold (required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for correlated inputs, use expert elicitation (e.g., Delphi) to quantify distributions where needed, and present probabilistic results clearly with graphs/tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption about risk preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: In combining probability distributions of outcomes, assume societal risk neutrality in general; if adopting a different risk preference, explain reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on expected (average) values is appropriate under risk neutrality, but analysts should state and justify any deviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make alternative assumptions explicit and test them
rubrics_metrics.description: If estimates depend heavily on assumptions, make them explicit and carry out sensitivity analyses using plausible alternatives; if rankings or net benefits change sign under plausible alternatives, conduct further analysis to determine appropriate assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze estimation methods for hidden assumptions and document them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that effects are not counted more than once across categories or in both numerator and denominator of ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, do not reduce gross costs by a monetary value of life extension if life-years are used as the effectiveness measure in the denominator of a CEA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct effectiveness measures carefully (prefer final outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer final outcomes (lives saved, life-years saved) over intermediate outputs (tons pollution reduced) when measuring effectiveness; where output quality varies, capture variability in outcome measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explanation for choice of effectiveness measures and ensure they reflect variation in value across outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate dominated alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing alternatives, eliminate inferior alternatives identified by principles of strong and weak dominance when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure mutual exclusivity or combinability of alternatives is considered when constructing incremental cost-effectiveness ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for monetized ancillary benefits in CEA
rubrics_metrics.description: When some ancillary benefits can be monetized but the primary effectiveness measure cannot, subtract monetized ancillary benefits from gross costs to yield net-cost for CEA; if some ancillary benefits cannot be monetized, acknowledge potential overstatement of cost-effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If net cost becomes negative (monetized ancillary benefits exceed costs), report that result and explain implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report alternatives' summary including qualitative factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a summary of benefit and cost estimates for each alternative, including qualitative and non-monetized factors, so readers can evaluate tradeoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an executive summary and standardized accounting statement to facilitate comparison across alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting statement format and categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major final rule, using categories: monetized benefits, annualized quantified-but-unmonetized benefits, unquantified benefits, monetized costs, annualized monetized costs, quantified-but-unmonetized costs, qualitative costs, and transfers (on-budget/off-budget).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report effects on State/local/tribal governments, small businesses, wages, and growth in the accounting statement with source citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rounding of estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect the precision in the analysis; e.g., $220 million implies rounding to nearest $10 million (+/- $5 million), $222 million implies rounding to nearest $1 million (+/- $0.5 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and document appropriate rounding consistent with implied precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate reporting and classification of transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Report transfers separately and avoid misclassifying transfer payments as benefits or costs; distinguish on-budget transfers from off-budget transfers and identify from whom to whom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If transfers have significant efficiency effects as well as distributional effects, report them and use multiple categories where necessary to describe redistributive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify effects on subnational governments, small business, wages and growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits, costs, and transfers received by State, local, and tribal governments and, to the extent feasible, effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that rules with annual costs less than $1 billion are likely to have minimal effect on economic growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with specialized statutory and executive order analytic requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional analyses are required by law or executive orders: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) for small entities, Unfunded Mandates Act (> $100M), Paperwork Reduction Act (information collections), Information Quality Guidelines, NEPA (environmental impact statements), Executive Order 13045 (impacts on children), Executive Order 13211 (energy effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare required statements (e.g., Statement of Energy Effects) and coordinate with agency offices (CIO, Chief Counsel for Advocacy, CEQ) as appropriate; post RFA when prepared and consult SBA Advocacy Office per EO 13272 and SBREFA where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Quality and documentation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and analysis supporting rules must meet agency and OMB information quality standards; provide specific references to data sources and documentation of models where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency CIO and the Statistical and Science Policy Branch of OMB's OIRA can provide assistance; include appendices and model documentation to support transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing mortality risk reductions — present alternative primary estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: When developing estimates for reductions in premature mortality risk, present alternative primary estimates using different values for valuing reductions in mortality risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sensitivity to alternative VSL (value of statistical life) or other mortality valuation approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal expert elicitation when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use expert solicitation methods (e.g., Delphi) to quantify probability distributions of key parameters when data gaps exist or when formal probabilistic analysis is conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine expert judgments with other data in Monte Carlo or other simulations; document elicitation methods and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for correlated inputs in probabilistic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to correlated inputs when conducting simulations; standard defaults may assume independence and produce misleading uncertainty intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a special effort to portray probabilistic results meaningfully and correct for correlation where present.
